newsitem.title: USA: New US fund launched from only index-linked bonds.
newsitem.headline: New US fund launched from only index-linked bonds.

text.p: Along with the U.S. Treasury's initial offering of inflation-protected notes on Wednesday, one West Coast mutual fund said it has launched a new fund that would feature only index-linked bonds.
Bill Gross, managing director of Pacific Investment Managing Co, said he bought $5.0 million of the new 10-year U.S. notes to start up the fund, called the "PIMCO Real Return Bond Fund."
He also said he bought another $100 million of the index-linked notes for other PIMCO accounts.
"I wish we bought the whole auction in retrospect," Gross said in an interview with Reuters, noting the profit the notes made in trading following the auction.
Reminded that government laws only allow one account to buy as much as one-third of an auction, Gross said "Then I wish we bought a third."

Like almost all bond players, Gross did not expect such great demand at Wednesday's auction and figured he could get the notes around the 3.50 percent rate the market figured they would be awarded at.

But a late surge of demand pushed the when-issued 10-year note down to around 3.449 percent -- where the issue was awarded. In late-day trading, the yield had fallen all the way down to 3.39 percent -- a nice-sized profit.
In all, there were roughly $40 billion in bids for just $7.0 billion in notes.
"That's a tremendous number," Gross said. "It surprised most everyone. Going into the auction, talk was for yield levels of 3.5 percent and a substantial tail. But that never happened."
Still, Gross said he is looking forward to building on the new inflation-protected bond fund.
"Today was just a starting point -- a seed," he said.
Gross said his goal was to buy inflation-protected bonds from other countries as well, such as Canada, the UK and New Zealand.
"Our intent is to move from one country to another for inflation protection all the way, where we can take advantage of higher real yields in various countries," he said.
At around 3.40 percent, the U.S. notes offer the lowest real yield of any nation's debt.
For example, Canadian real yields are about 4.17 percent, albeit with a longer maturity. and New Zealand's inflation-protected bonds offer more than 4.50 percent, Gross noted.
"They are not apples to apples, but they are all inflation protected," he said. "This fund can grow to hundreds of millions of dollars. In a few months, we could be talking those numbers."
